To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women's work in agricultural production is not associated with higher food intakes, but is associated with lower energy intakes and lower feeding practices, and that these negative associations are mediated by seasonality and social identity.

women in India's agricultural households work long hours in agriculture and domestic reproduction, that this work is gendered and seasonal, and that it has a negative impact on women's nutrition and health and on child feeding and care practices.

women's agricultural work has both positive and negative implications on nutrition through two key pathways: (i) increased control over income, which can be used to purchase nutritious food; and (ii) increased work burdens, which can lead to reduced time for care work and energy deficits, which in turn can affect their own health and the nutritional status of their children.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the gender dimensions of the relationship between agriculture and nutrition, and in particular, with the ways in which gendered social relations shape women's work in agricultural production and its implications for nutrition.
the gendered nature of agricultural work in the context of seasonality and its impact on women’s own health, as well as on their ability to care for their children.
the gendered time and seasonality of agricultural production and the implications of this time and seasonality for nutrition outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women's participation in agricultural activities has a negative effect on nutrition.
the evidence on the link between agriculture and nutrition through women's agricultural work is weak and inconclusive, and more research is needed.
women's agricultural labor is associated with lower nutritional status, and this is due to the fact that women are often the last to eat and the last to get food.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gendered time is a critical determinant of women's nutritional well-being and that of their families.
gender equality and women's empowerment are key for achieving food security, nutrition, and improved health for all.
women's work is not necessarily bad for nutrition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women's work is not just an input into agriculture, but also an output of agriculture that needs to be recognized and supported.
the seasonality of agricultural work is an important factor to consider in the design of nutrition interventions.
gendered time and seasonality matter for nutrition.
